title: #diastasisrecti: a mixed-methods analysis of Instagram posts and their influence on women's exercise and sports participation
screen_reason: Part 1 is a quantitative content analysis of Instagram posts with an explicit denominator: of the 28 eligible #diastasisrecti posts giving exercise/sports suggestions, 17 (60.7%) gave suggestions 'currently not supported by the literature' when compared against an expert-synthesised evidence framework. That is a share of items judged against an external evidence standard and reported as a share, so CONTENT (flagged borderline - see the row notes on the evidence-based/non-evidence-based label). Part 2 is qualitative (20 interviews) and yields no clean share of respondents who encountered misinformation.

estimates.country: not stated for posts (English-language posts only; author team Italy/Spain/USA/UK)
estimates.measure_type: % of eligible #diastasisrecti Instagram posts whose exercise and sports suggestions for women with diastasis recti were not supported by the current evidence
estimates.value_raw: 17 (60.7%) of 28 posts non-evidence-based vs 11 (39.3%) evidence-based (Table 1); abstract: "The majority (61%, n = 17) provided non-evidence-based suggestions"
estimates.denominator: 28 public Instagram posts eligible for inclusion (those containing exercise/sports suggestions, indications or contraindications for women with DRA), screened from the first 1,000 posts tagged #diastasisrecti on 1 June 2023
estimates.definition: the post's exercise and sports suggestions, compared item by item against an evidence-based framework synthesised from the DRA literature (prioritising RCTs and systematic reviews), were categorised 'non-evidence-based'
estimates.misinfo_def: No formal definition of misinformation. Operationally: "IG content related to exercise and sports suggestions was synthesized and systematically compared by SG and SS with the framework outlined in Supplementary File 2. Based on this comparison, content was categorized as 'evidence-based' or 'non-evidence-based'." The discussion characterises this content as misinformation: "The impact of such content ranges from confusion and misinformation to nocebo effects".

estimates.ground_truth_detail: Two authors (a physiotherapist-researcher and a colleague) independently screened the 1,000 posts, disagreements resolved by a third author; content was then compared by the same two authors against an evidence-based framework built by narrative synthesis of the most recent and methodologically robust DRA studies, prioritising RCTs and systematic reviews (Supplementary File 2). No kappa or percentage-agreement statistic is reported for the evidence-based/non-evidence-based coding itself.
estimates.moderator_quote: the most relevant and popular discussions, the first 1,000
estimates.notes: JUDGEMENT CALLS for the adjudicator. (1) CONSTRUCT: the numerator label is 'not supported by the literature', not 'false' or 'inaccurate'. Strictly, a wholly correct suggestion could be labelled non-evidence-based simply because no trial has tested it, which is the test that normally pushes a row to QUALITY. I coded CONTENT because (a) the judgement is made on the CLAIMS themselves against an expert-synthesised evidence base, which the rules admit as expert verification/guideline concordance, (b) the discussion makes clear the discordant content actively contradicts the evidence ('current categorical assertions that label exercises or sports activities as "safe," "harmful," or "avoid" lack robust scientific support') and is described as misinformation with nocebo effects, and (c) this paper keeps the two axes separate itself - veracity is the evidence-based coding, information QUALITY is the QUEST score, reported separately. borderline = true so this can be flipped to QUALITY if the project's rule is stricter. (2) DENOMINATOR: 60.7% is a share of the 28 ELIGIBLE posts, not of the 1,000 screened - only posts that actually gave exercise/sports advice were eligible, so this is not '61% of #diastasisrecti content is misinformation'. The 28/1000 filtering rate matters for any pooled estimate. (3) The sample is small (n=28), rank-truncated (first 1,000 tagged posts), public accounts only, English only, and excludes stories and reels, which the authors note the algorithm preferentially promotes. (4) breadth = misleading rather than false: the numerator is unsupported/overconfident prescriptive advice, not fabricated claims.

missed_or_uncertain: (1) NO RECALL row was entered from Part 2, though it was considered carefully. The interview study (n = 20 purposively sampled, English-speaking women with a clinician diagnosis of DRA, recruited through the first author's own Instagram campaign) reports three mutually exclusive recall categories: 'Four women out of 20 (20%) recalled solely evidence-based content', 'The majority (n = 8; 40%) remembered assertive content, including do/do not do lists', and 'Six participants (30%) mentioned contrasting and opposing suggestions, including both evidence and non-evidence-based'. None of these is a clean 'share of respondents who encountered misinformation': the 40% category is defined by TONE (assertiveness), the 30% category by CONTRADICTION, and the obvious misinformation figure (80% = everyone who did not recall solely evidence-based content) would be a complement I computed, which R8 forbids. The sample is also a self-selected qualitative sample recruited from a DRA-focused Instagram account, so any share would be near-uninterpretable as prevalence. Recorded here in full so an adjudicator can decide. (2) QUEST quality results are not entered as rows: the total score is reported only as a median (10 of 28, IQR 4), which the rules exclude as a scale mean with no share; its sub-items ARE reported as shares - 'Tone': 20 (71.7%) of creators "fully and unequivocally supported their claims and information" (restated later as "20 of the included posts (71.1%) were characterized by assertive tones" - the paper gives 71.7% and 71.1% for what is 20/28 = 71.4%), one (3.6%) gave balanced information with caution, and 'Attribution': only 2 of 28 (7.1%) mentioned an expert/scientific source. These are presentation-quality items (tone, sourcing), not veracity, so they were left out for the same reason PEMAT items were left out elsewhere; they would be QUALITY rows if wanted. (3) 'aggressive marketing tactics... were present in approximately half of the analysed posts' - commercial bias, not misinformation, and only approximate. (4) Account and post descriptors (6 of 28 verified accounts, 7 profiles with >50,000 followers, median 2,316 followers, format breakdown) carry no misinformation share. (5) Participant characteristics in Table 3 are sample descriptors. (6) The background DRA prevalence figures (45% and 33% of postpartum women) are the medical condition's prevalence cited from other papers, not misinformation, and are excluded by R8 anyway. (7) Figure 2 (comparative summary of evidence-based vs non-evidence-based content across posts and interviews, 'along with their respective prevalence') is an image and could not be read; it may contain additional percentages an adjudicator with the PDF should check. Supplementary Files 4, 5a-c and 8 hold the post-level analysis and were not available in this text. (8) QUOTE PROVENANCE: this PDF extracts as interleaved two-column lines, so most running-text sentences are not contiguous in the text file (and words are hyphen-split across lines, e.g. 'dissemi-/nated'). Every source_quote, moderator_quote and rob quote above is a span that is contiguous in the file, which is why some end mid-sentence; the fuller wording quoted in the definition and misinfo_def fields is the paper's own, reassembled across those breaks. Note also that Table 1 prints the figure as '17 (60.7)' without a percent sign.

rob.design: Convergent parallel mixed-methods study, protocol registered, ethics approval Cardiff Metropolitan University (Sta-7673), reported per GRAMMS. PART 1 (the quantitative arm): convenience sample of public, English-language Instagram posts; the first 1,000 posts tagged #diastasisrecti were retrieved with an IG Hashtag Scraper on 1 June 2023 by two authors independently (pilot search 31 March 2023 confirmed consistency), screened for eligibility by the same two authors with a third resolving disagreements, leaving 28 posts; stories, reels, live registrations, non-English and duplicate posts excluded. Content was compared against an evidence framework synthesised from the DRA literature and coded evidence-based vs non-evidence-based; information quality was scored with QUEST (max 28). No inter-rater reliability coefficient is reported for either coding step, verbatim post text could not be published for ethics reasons, and analysis was restricted to public accounts. PART 2: worldwide Instagram recruitment campaign from the first author's account, July 2023 - May 2024; 31 women completed the survey, 11 did not respond to scheduling, and 20 semi-structured interviews were conducted until saturation; Braun & Clarke thematic analysis by two independent coders with investigator triangulation, member checking and audit trail. Acknowledged limitations: the included sample may not represent the platform's content diversity, excluding reels/videos may misrepresent what the algorithm promotes, and nationalities were unevenly represented among interviewees.
